A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same inference-set-design study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on MNIST variants, QM9, Molecules3D, RxRx3, and a proprietary phenomics dataset, including acquisition curves and analyses of difficult examples.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical studies and reports additional comparator results, calibration analyses, chemical-element coverage analysis, and repeated-trial evaluations of stopping accuracy.

M1.justification: The core hybrid-screening procedure, least-confidence/QBC acquisition, and KL-based classification stopping remain. v2 Appendix E.1 adds a regression-specific stopping procedure requiring acquired-batch MSE below a threshold for a patience period. Algorithm 1 also corrects label acquisition and explicitly removes acquired examples, aligning its pseudocode with operations already described in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same MNIST variants, QM9 classification, Molecules3D HOMO-LUMO-gap and energy regression, RxRx3, and proprietary phenomics task. Molecules3D moves into Appendix E.1; the new diagnostic analyses use retained datasets and task conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds BALD, diversity sampling, and SA-score ordering to the QM9 and biological classification comparisons, substantially expanding v1's random and limited ordering baselines. Molecules3D additionally compares SA-score and large-to-small ordering against the retained QBC, random, and small-to-large methods. These methods appear in the reported curves, not merely citations.

E3.justification: The reported QM9 acquisition batch changes from 50 to 250 between v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2. v2 introduces regression stopping evaluations with patience 10 and MSE thresholds of 0.1 and 100 eV^2, plus a separate stopping-validation protocol using delta = 0.05 and dataset-specific accuracy targets. Existing dataset splits and network sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of weak calibration throughout acquisition, empirical checks of accuracy at stopping, and an analysis of chemical-element coverage explaining failures of large-to-small molecular acquisition (Figures 9, 11, 13, and 14). The earlier MNIST corruption analyses and QM9 difficult-example tracking are retained, with the latter extended to more acquisition methods.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-seed benchmark experiments. v2 explicitly identifies curve shading as standard error and stopping-time intervals as minimum-to-maximum ranges. Its separate stopping-validation study uses 100 seeds for MNIST variants and QM9 and 50 for phenomics, reporting empirical failure frequencies; this is not a blanket increase in repetitions for all existing experiments.

E6.justification: v2 substantially expands comparator and diagnostic outcomes. QM9 active/LC and random savings are replaced from 54.6%/23.2% in v1 Figure 6 to 53.6%/16.6% in v2 Figure 5 under changed batch settings. New regression stopping results report QBC savings of 21.3% and 20.2%. Figure 14 reports no LC stopping failures and random-agent failure rates of 1% on MNIST and 6% on QM9.

T1.justification: v2 reformulates weak calibration using multiclass top-prediction confidence and replaces v1's short, internally inconsistent proof with an explicit ordered-confidence argument in Appendix A.1. This corrects the inequality direction used in v1 Appendix D. Appendix A.2 additionally derives the Chernoff/KL confidence bound instead of only citing a concentration result.

C1.justification: The central claims about finite-library hybrid screening, pruning difficult examples, and reducing acquisition costs remain. v2's expanded Section 5 adds a broader concluding claim that heuristic acquisition orderings can be highly suboptimal and introduce biases that undermine performance estimation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting heuristic failures to chemical-element coverage and selection bias, and explains why least-confidence selection permits conservative performance estimation. It also explicitly identifies perfectly accurate, deterministic observed labels as a limitation for noisy biological experiments. The earlier limitation concerning low predictive power on RxRx3 is retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds grid-search guidance for computing the confidence bound, specifies regression stopping parameters, and describes diversity selection through Tanimoto distance. Most preprocessing and architectural details are retained or relocated, alongside the reported QM9 batch-size revision. Code remains promised upon publication, and the proprietary dataset remains unavailable.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chernoff (1952) and Guo et al. (2017) on calibration, and removes Yang and Loog (2018). The substantive positioning relative to active learning, Bayesian optimization, and core-set selection in Section 3 remains essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the stopping-criterion exposition and reorganizes supporting material: theory becomes the first appendix, preprocessing is consolidated, and Molecules3D results move out of the main text. It adds Section 4.4 and expands the former conclusion into a discussion. These structural changes accompany wording and terminology revisions throughout.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the introductory schematic and reworks benchmark plots with additional method curves, expanded legends, revised axes, and stopping-time intervals. It adds calibration panels, a chemical-element coverage plot, and stopping-accuracy violin plots. The Molecules3D display moves to the appendix, while both existing tables are retained and reordered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central stopping rule. Compared with v1's inconsistent calibration statement, sketch proof, and untested calibration assumption, it provides a clearer formal treatment, calibration diagnostics, and extensive repeated-trial stopping evaluations. Broader evaluated baselines and an explicit perfect-label limitation also improve the credibility and scope of interpretation. These gains address central evidential gaps, although code access remains promised and the proprietary data remain unavailable.
